body.heading: Metal delivered by electricity
paragraphs: Electroplating coats an object with a thin layer of metal using an electric current — electrolysis working in reverse gear. Instead of splitting a compound apart, it persuades metal to leave a solution and settle, atom by atom, onto a surface, building a coating that can be far thinner than a human hair yet completely continuous.

The reason the coating lands where it does is charge. The dissolved metal exists in the bath as positively charged ions, and opposite charges attract: give the object a negative charge and the ions migrate to it, gain electrons, and turn back into solid metal exactly where they touch.

body.heading: The plating bath, step by step
paragraphs: First the object is cleaned until it is spotless, because plating faithfully copies whatever lies beneath, including dirt. Then it is wired to the negative terminal of a power supply, making it the cathode, and lowered into a solution containing a salt of the coating metal.

The positive terminal connects to a bar of the coating metal itself, the anode. Switch on, and two things happen in balance: metal ions plate onto the object, while atoms from the anode bar dissolve to replace them, keeping the bath topped up. Leave the current running longer, or run it stronger, and the coating grows thicker.

body.heading: Chrome taps and golden connectors
paragraphs: Look around and plating is everywhere. The mirror shine on a bathroom tap is chromium, usually laid over layers of nickel and copper on cheaper metal beneath. Silver-plated cutlery is a base metal wearing a precious skin, and the inside of a food can carries a whisper-thin coat of tin to keep the steel from reacting with the contents.

Engineers plate for performance as much as beauty. The connectors inside phones and computers are often gold-plated — not for show, but because gold refuses to corrode, so the electrical contact stays clean for years.
